nameStory: The hoop-petticoat daffodil gets its charming name from its distinctive flower shape that looks exactly like a Victorian-era petticoat or hoop skirt! The trumpet-shaped center (called a corona) flares out dramatically like fabric stretched over a wire hoop frame. This whimsical resemblance made the name stick among gardeners who delighted in its dainty, dress-like appearance.
description: The hoop-petticoat daffodil is a small, delicate bulb flower that stands out from typical daffodils with its unique funnel-shaped bloom. Instead of the usual flat petals surrounding a trumpet center, this charming plant has tiny, narrow petals that are completely overshadowed by an enormous, flared corona that dominates the flower. Growing only 4-6 inches tall, it's one of the smallest members of the daffodil family. Originally from southwestern Europe, it's extremely rare in New England gardens and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - a dramatically flared, trumpet-shaped corona (center) that's much wider than it is tall, resembling a tiny yellow funnel or bell. The six petals are extremely narrow and pointed, almost thread-like, and are completely dwarfed by the large corona.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow color throughout, with the corona often having a slightly deeper, more saturated yellow than the thin petals. Each stem typically carries just one flower that nods slightly downward.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, grass-like leaves that are almost thread-thin and bluish-green in color. They feel smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch, emerging directly from the base of the plant in a small clump.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely small and delicate overall appearance, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height. The entire plant has a miniature, almost fairy-like quality that makes it easy to overlook among other spring flowers.

habitat: In New England, hoop-petticoat daffodils are extremely rare and found only in specialized rock gardens or collections of bulb enthusiasts. When they do appear, they prefer well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils in sunny locations that mimic their native Mediterranean climate. They may occasionally naturalize in abandoned garden sites or old estates where they were originally planted.

seasonality.spring: Blooms very early in spring, often in March or early April, with the distinctive funnel-shaped flowers appearing before most other daffodils. The narrow, grass-like foliage emerges at the same time as the flowers.
seasonality.summer: Foliage dies back completely by early summer, leaving no visible trace above ground. The bulb remains dormant underground during the hot, dry summer months.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts. This is actually the best time to plant bulbs if you can find them from specialty suppliers.
seasonality.winter: No visible growth above ground, though the bulb may begin developing roots in late winter in preparation for spring emergence.

funFact: This tiny daffodil is so perfectly adapted to windy mountain slopes in its native Spain and Portugal that its enormous corona actually acts like a megaphone, amplifying the flower's faint fragrance to attract pollinators across great distances!
confusionNotes: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, it's unlikely to be confused with anything else once you see that distinctive mega-corona! If you think you've found one, you've probably discovered something quite special - or it might be a different small yellow flower like winter aconite, which has multiple small petals arranged in a flat circle rather than the daffodil's trumpet structure.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "daffodil," many people don't realize that all daffodils are actually narcissus - the terms are interchangeable! The extreme rarity of this species in New England means any sighting would be noteworthy and worth reporting to local botanical groups.
compareHints: Unlike other daffodils in New England, the hoop-petticoat has an enormous corona that completely dominates tiny, thread-like petals - the exact opposite of poet's narcissus which has huge white petals and a tiny orange cup. Wild daffodils and other common species have more balanced proportions between petals and corona, while this species looks like someone inflated just the trumpet part of the flower to comical proportions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the familiar yellow trumpet daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) that bloom earlier, poet's narcissus has pure white petals and a flat, small center rather than a large trumpet.

Wild daffodil differs from its Narcissus relatives by having pale yellow petals rather than the pure white of Poet's Narcissus or Paperwhite, and produces single flowers rather than the clusters seen in Bunch-flowered Daffodil.
Unlike wild daffodil which has one large flower per stem, this species always has multiple smaller flowers clustered together.
Unlike other New England daffodils that bloom singly in spring with thick, substantial petals, paperwhite produces clusters of smaller flowers with distinctively thin, translucent petals.
Angel's-tears differs from other New England daffodils by its tiny size, pure white color, and distinctly drooping flowers.
